claims.text: The equiatomic quinary Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy has enhanced mechanical properties compared with its equiatomic quaternary and ternary subsets.
Greater chemical complexity in the quinary alloy produces increased atomic-scale lattice distortion.
Atomic-scale lattice distortions alter stacking-fault energy.
Atomic-scale lattice distortions alter dislocation mobility during deformation.
The distortion-mediated changes in stacking-fault energy and dislocation mobility improve yield strength and strain hardening and delay failure.
The quinary, quaternary, and ternary formulations can be prepared as single-phase FCC alloys using identical thermomechanical processing.
Processing conditions, grain size, and phase uniformity will be held constant while comparing quinary, quaternary, and ternary alloys.
The quinary alloy has greater atomic-size mismatch and more pronounced lattice distortion than the quaternary and ternary alloys.
The more pronounced lattice distortion in the quinary alloy modifies dislocation nucleation and mobility.
Modified dislocation nucleation and mobility in the quinary alloy enhance yield strength and strain hardening and delay the onset of plastic instability.
Relative to the quinary baseline, the quaternary and ternary alloys will have lower yield strength.
Relative to the quinary baseline, the quaternary and ternary alloys will have lower strain-hardening rates.
Relative to the quinary baseline, the quaternary and ternary alloys will fail earlier under identical deformation conditions.
The equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni baseline exhibits pronounced lattice distortion and superior mechanical performance.
The proposed mechanism applies to room-temperature uniaxial tension of single-phase FCC alloys with matched thermomechanical processing and grain size.
